questions.question: Why should AI-Enhanced User Research be taught as a workflow instead of only as tool awareness?
options: Because AI-generated personas are automatically representative of the whole user base
Because polished, confident-sounding quotes are proof the sample size was sufficient
Because teams need shared signals, controls, and decision rules they can apply to real work
Because a single synthesis pass removes the need for running any further round of user interviews
questions.explanation: The lesson is built around reusable operating artifacts — not the idea that generated personas are automatically representative, that confident quotes prove sample size, or that one synthesis pass replaces further interviews.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, what does the AI miss when it turns raw interview notes into confident personas?
options: The interview transcripts were altogether far too short to generate any personas worth using at all
The assistant refused outright to produce any quotes without first putting a signed data-processing agreement in place
The generated personas were technically accurate but written in the wrong language for the target market
Personal data in the notes, a sample skewed toward power users, and disagreement flattened into confident segments
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening example shows AI missing exactly this: personal data buried in notes, a sample skewed toward power users, and real disagreement flattened into tidy, confident personas — not a transcript-length problem, a compliance refusal, or a language mismatch.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce for AI-Enhanced User Research?
options: A fully anonymized transcript ready to publish without further review
A single sentiment score with no link back to the underlying evidence or transcript
A ranked plan with category, score, priority, controls, and rationale
A slide deck summarizing the interviews for a leadership readout
questions.explanation: The lesson's Python artifact outputs a ranked plan — category, score, priority, controls, and rationale — not a pre-anonymized transcript, an unlinked sentiment score, or a leadership slide deck.

questions.question: Which control belongs to the lesson design?
options: Anonymization, so personal data in interview notes never reaches a persona or a slide
Publishing quotes with names attached because the assistant already redacted them
Skipping evidence tags since the interview sample felt representative enough
Treating a single power-user complaint as proof of a wider product problem
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls include anonymization — keeping personal data out of personas and slides — the opposite of trusting the assistant's own redaction, skipping evidence tags, or treating one complaint as broad proof.

questions.question: When should a scenario become a launch-gate discussion rather than a casual awareness exercise?
options: Only when the interview sample happens to already include some enterprise customers
Only when the resulting personas are going to be shown directly to external stakeholders in a readout
When impact, uncertainty, and matched risk signals such as personal data are all running high
Never — a research synthesis gap can always wait for the next round of user interviews
questions.explanation: High-impact, uncertain, risk-heavy research findings need a launch gate regardless of who's in the sample, who sees the personas, or whether another interview round is scheduled.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the output template?
options: To formally replace the researcher's own judgment about what counts as valid evidence
To keep unresolved contradictions in the interview data hidden from the product team
To automatically generate completion certificates for participants once the workshop ends
To create a reusable worksheet or prompt teams keep applying after the course ends
questions.explanation: The output template is meant to become a reusable worksheet or prompt teams keep applying — not a substitute for researcher judgment, a way to hide contradictions, or an automatic certificate generator.
